opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I see it, the starting point was a pretty practical question: can we get most of the efficiency of linear attention without paying the usual price in quality, especially on things like long-context retrieval and in-context recall, where pure linear models have historically struggled?

Early on, a lot of the community's experiments with hybrids were somewhat ad hoc. People would take a linear layer, maybe Mamba-style or a gated linear attention variant, interleave it with full attention at some ratio, and see what happened. The general finding was encouraging: you don't need full attention everywhere. A small fraction of global attention layers seems to handle the precise retrieval, and the linear layers do a lot of the heavy lifting for local and compressive modeling.

What I find interesting about the Kimi line of work is that they didn't just treat the linear part as a cheap filler. They put real effort into making the linear layer itself stronger. The direction built on the delta rule, the gated DeltaNet family, where instead of just accumulating key-value outer products into the state, you do something closer to an online regression update, so the model can overwrite or correct what's stored. Then they made the gating more fine-grained, so different channels can decay at different rates rather than one scalar gate for the whole head. That gives the recurrent state much better control over what it keeps and what it forgets.

Once the linear layer is that much stronger, the hybrid ratio question changes. You can push toward something like three linear layers for every full-attention layer and still match or even beat a full-attention baseline in their controlled comparisons, while cutting KV cache a lot and speeding up long-context decoding. And in some setups they even found you could drop explicit positional encoding on the full-attention layers, because the linear layers already carry positional and recency information through their gating. That's a nice example of the two components actually specializing rather than just coexisting.

So in terms of progression, I'd describe it as moving from "hybrid as a compromise," where linear attention is the weak but cheap part, toward "hybrid as a co-design," where the linear layer is expressive enough to be a first-class citizen, and the full-attention layers are kept mainly for the things they're uniquely good at. The other thing I'd emphasize is that none of this matters without the systems side: chunkwise parallel algorithms and efficient kernels so the linear layers actually train fast on GPUs. A lot of the early progress was really about making these architectures hardware-friendly enough that people could run serious scaling experiments at all.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest way to describe it is that the design didn't start from an elegant idea, it started from a constraint. We knew from the very beginning that if you want a model to go to a million-token context, or even to serve agents that are making dozens of tool calls in a single trajectory, full attention everywhere becomes a KV cache problem and a decoding speed problem before it becomes a quality problem. So the question was never "is linear attention better than softmax attention." The question was "how much full attention can we take out before the model stops being a good model."

The first experiments were really just interleaving. You take a standard Transformer, you replace some fraction of the layers with a linear attention variant, and you look at what happens to the loss curve and to the long-context evals. And the early results were kind of humbling, honestly. If you use a naive linear attention, something like the original kernelized form with no gating and no forgetting mechanism, the model is fine on short-context language modeling but it falls apart on retrieval. It can't look something up precisely because the state is a fixed-size matrix and everything gets smeared together.

So the progression in my mind is really a progression of the recurrent part getting smarter. The gating was the first big step. Once you have a data-dependent decay, the model can decide what to forget, and the long-context behavior improves a lot. Then the delta-rule style updates, where instead of just accumulating key-value outer products you actually correct the state, you subtract out what was there and write in the new value. That is what we built on for Kimi Linear with the KDA layer. The intuition is that the state behaves much more like a fast weight that is being trained online, rather than a bucket that is filling up.

And the second axis of progression is the ratio. Early on people were fairly conservative, maybe one-to-one, half full attention and half linear. What we found in scaling experiments is that you can push much further than that, something like three linear layers for every full attention layer, and the full attention layers carry the precise retrieval while the linear layers do most of the in-context computation. At that point the KV cache is reduced by a large factor, decoding gets dramatically faster at long context, and on the benchmarks the hybrid is actually matching or beating the full-attention baseline at the same training budget, which was not something I expected to see so cleanly.

The part I'd emphasize is that none of this was obvious from small-scale experiments alone. A lot of linear attention papers, including some of my own earlier work, look great at 300 million or 1 billion parameters and then you don't know what happens beyond that. What Kimi's setup gave us was the ability to run these ablations at a scale where the answer actually matters, with the same data and the same training recipe as the production models. So I'd say the design progressed less because of one clever idea and more because we could afford to be empirically disciplined about it: change one thing, scale it up, see whether retrieval and reasoning hold, and only keep what survives.

astra-6.text: I’d frame it as a gradual exploration of where full attention is necessary and where a more efficient mechanism can take its place. The key question is how to reduce the cost of attention while preserving the model’s ability to use context. But we haven’t established the details of Kimi’s initial experiments here, so I can’t confidently describe their sequence or say what each stage demonstrated.

sol-6.1.text: I’d be careful about describing a specific progression without the experimental details. At a high level, hybrid attention explores how to combine attention mechanisms with different strengths—for example, using full attention to preserve access to the broader context while using a more efficient mechanism elsewhere. The early experiments would help establish how much of that efficiency you can gain without losing model quality. But we haven’t established which variants Kimi tried first or what those experiments showed, so I can’t give a reliable chronology.
